15310: At the heart of every use of "strip" is one powerful idea: removal that leaves something bare, exposed, or empty. When you strip something, you are not just taking a little away — you are removing a layer, a covering, a possession, or a quality, often completely. Think of it as peeling away until what remains is raw and uncovered.

1. To Remove Clothing

The most familiar use of "strip" is to take clothes off — either your own or someone else's.

  • She stripped off her wet jacket the moment she got home.
  • The doctor asked him to strip to the waist so she could examine his back.
  • He stripped and jumped into the river.

Notice that "strip" suggests removing clothes quickly or completely, not just loosening a button. It carries a sense of thorough removal. The phrase "strip down" is very common here and means to undress to minimal or no clothing: "They stripped down before getting into the pool."

A "stripper" is a person who removes their clothes as a performance — this comes directly from this meaning.

2. To Remove a Surface Layer or Covering from Something

You can strip a surface — meaning you remove whatever is coating it to expose what lies underneath.

  • We stripped the old paint from the walls before repainting.
  • He spent the afternoon stripping wallpaper from the bedroom.
  • The deer had stripped the bark off several trees.
  • Strip the leaves from the stems before putting the flowers in a vase.

The key here is that something on top of or around another thing is being removed. The wall, tree, or stem still exists — you are just removing what was covering it.

3. To Remove Everything from a Place or Object

"Strip" can also mean to take everything out of or off something, leaving it completely bare or empty — like a skeleton picked clean.

  • Thieves broke in and stripped the apartment of every valuable item.
  • The mechanics stripped the old car down to its bare frame.
  • Locusts stripped the fields, leaving nothing behind.

This meaning often appears with the phrase "strip something of something" — meaning to remove all contents or all value from it. It has a sense of thoroughness bordering on destruction.

4. To Take Away a Title, Right, Rank, or Privilege

Here, "strip" is used figuratively for taking something abstract away from someone — something they have earned, hold, or own by status.

  • The court stripped him of his citizenship.
  • She was stripped of her gold medal after failing the drugs test.
  • The scandal led to the general being stripped of his rank.
  • The new law stripped citizens of several key protections.

The structure is almost always: strip someone of something. The thing being taken away is not physical — it is a title, a status, a right, or a privilege. Notice how this carries a harsh tone: stripping something from someone implies that the removal is forceful, often punitive, and leaves them diminished or exposed — just like the other meanings of the word.

5. To Damage the Threads of a Screw or Gear (Mechanical)

In mechanics and engineering, you can "strip" a screw, bolt, or gear. This means the grooves (called threads) on the screw or the teeth on the gear get worn down or broken — usually from too much force or using the wrong tool.

  • Be careful not to overtighten it or you'll strip the screw.
  • He used too much force and stripped the bolt.
  • The gearbox failed because a gear had been stripped.

A stripped screw is essentially ruined — it can no longer be tightened or loosened properly because the grooves that a screwdriver grips are gone. The word fits perfectly: the screw has been "stripped" of the very feature that made it functional.

6. To Remove Insulation from a Wire (Electrical)

This is a specific but very common technical use. An electrical wire is usually coated in a protective layer of rubber or plastic. Before you can connect a wire to anything, you must remove that coating at the end to expose the metal conductor inside.

  • Use wire strippers to strip the ends of the cable.
  • He stripped about two centimetres of insulation from each wire.

This is simply a specialized version of meaning #2 — removing a coating to expose what's underneath — but it appears so frequently in everyday contexts (home repairs, electronics, etc.) that it is worth knowing separately.

7. To Separate Something from Something Else

More broadly, "strip" can mean to separate a substance or element from whatever it is attached to or mixed with — common in cooking, farming, and industry.

  • Strip the corn kernels off the cob.
  • The machine strips seeds from the raw cotton.
  • Strip the meat from the bones.

Again, the idea is the same: you are removing one thing from another, leaving them separated.

"Strip away" — to remove something in order to reveal what is truly underneath. This is often used figuratively to cut through complexity or pretense:

  • If you strip away all the complicated language, the argument is actually very simple.
  • Grief can strip away everything you thought was important.

"Strip down" — to reduce something to only its most basic and essential form:

  • Let's strip down this plan to what really matters.
  • The engineers stripped down the engine to diagnose the problem.

"Strip" almost always implies that what remains after the action is bare, raw, and exposed. Whether it's a person without clothes, a wall without paint, a soldier without rank, or a field without crops — something has been removed and what is left behind is unprotected and uncovered. This gives the word a slight edge: it is more forceful and more complete than softer words like remove or take off. When something is stripped, it is not gently unwrapped — it is fully and thoroughly cleared.
15311:
Picture dragging a wet paintbrush once across a white wall. You'd leave a long, narrow band of color — that is a stripe. A stripe is a long, narrow band that stands out from what surrounds it, usually because of a difference in color, shade, or sometimes texture. It is always much longer than it is wide, it has two relatively clear edges running along its length, and it contrasts with what's beside it.

That contrast is the soul of the word. A stripe isn't just any line — it is a visible band that you can distinguish from its background. Remove the contrast, and there is no stripe.

This is how most people use the word most of the time: a stripe is a band of a different color running across or through something.

  • A zebra's coat has alternating black and white stripes.
  • The American flag has thirteen red and white horizontal stripes.
  • A bumblebee has yellow and black stripes on its body.
  • A referee's shirt often has bold stripes across it.
  • A stripe of golden sunlight crept across the floor as the curtain moved.

Things that have many repeating stripes are called striped. But a single one is still called "a stripe."

Stripes can run in any direction — horizontally, vertically, or diagonally. What makes them stripes is not their direction but their shape: narrow, elongated, and contrasting with the background.
Stripe as a Mark of Rank

In the military, police forces, and other uniformed organizations, the word "stripe" refers specifically to the chevron-shaped or bar-shaped marks on a uniform — usually stitched onto the sleeve or shoulder — that show a person's rank. The more stripes, the higher the rank. A new recruit may have none; a sergeant may wear three.

This gives rise to one of the most common expressions in English: "earn your stripes." Literally, it meant earning the rank-indicating stripes sewn onto your uniform sleeve. Figuratively — and this is how it is almost always used today — it means to prove yourself through real effort and experience, to demonstrate that you have genuinely earned your place. A young doctor who has worked grueling hours in a hospital and handled difficult cases has "earned her stripes." A journalist who has covered wars and broken important stories has "earned his stripes."

This is a figurative use of the word, but it appears very frequently in writing and conversation. When people talk about someone's stripe, they mean their type, sort, or variety — especially in terms of beliefs, outlook, or character.

  • "Politicians of every stripe gathered for the debate." — meaning politicians of all kinds: conservative, liberal, independent, and so on.
  • "I don't associate with people of that stripe." — meaning people of that particular type or character.
  • "Artists of a different stripe see creativity differently." — meaning artists of a different kind or approach.

This sense comes from the same place as the others: a stripe is a distinguishing mark. Just as you can identify a species or rank by its markings, you can identify a person's "stripe" — their category — by the traits that define them.
The Old, Rare Meaning: A Blow or Its Mark

In older texts — particularly older Bible translations, classical literature, and historical writing — "stripe" sometimes means a stroke delivered by a whip or cane, or the mark (a raised welt or wound) left on the skin by such a blow. You might read in an old translation: "He received forty stripes." This means forty lashes.

This meaning is essentially dead in modern everyday English. You will not hear it in conversation. But you may encounter it in historical or religious texts, so it is worth knowing.

These two words are easily confused because they look and sound so similar.

A strip (no e at the end) refers to a narrow piece of something — a physical sliver or slice. A strip of paper. A strip of bacon. A landing strip at an airport. The word focuses on the shape of the object itself.

A stripe, by contrast, focuses on a visual marking — a band of contrasting color or pattern on a surface. The stripe isn't a separate piece; it's something you see on something. A tiger's stripes are not strips of fur peeled off — they are color patterns on the fur.

That said, in informal speech, the two words are sometimes used interchangeably for narrow bands of color, and most people won't correct you either way.

"Stars and Stripes" — The well-known nickname for the American flag, referring to its stars and its horizontal stripes.

"Earn your stripes" — To prove yourself through hard work and real experience; to show you deserve your position.

"Of every stripe" / "of all stripes" — Of every kind, type, or variety. "People of all stripes came to the festival" means people of every background and type attended.

"Of a different stripe" — Of a different kind or character. "She's a writer of a different stripe" means she approaches writing in a noticeably distinct way compared to others.

The word "stripe" always carries the same basic picture beneath all its uses: something long, narrow, and visibly distinct from what surrounds it. Whether it is a band of color on an animal's coat, a rank marking on a soldier's sleeve, or a figurative "type" of person identified by their characteristic traits, the underlying idea is the same — a stripe is something that sets one thing apart from another and makes it recognizable for what it is.
15312:
A stripling is a boy or young male who is on the edge of becoming a man — but isn't quite there yet. Think of a teenager, roughly 13 to 18 years old, who has started to grow tall but still looks young, lean, and undeveloped compared to a full-grown adult man.

The word captures that specific in-between stage: no longer a little child, but not yet a mature man. He might be tall, but he's slim and not yet physically filled out. He might be eager, but he lacks the deep experience that comes with age.

When people use this word, they usually have a few things in mind at once:

  • Youth — He is visibly young. You can tell just by looking at him.
  • Slenderness — He is slim, lean, and slight in build. Not yet broad-shouldered or muscular like a grown man.
  • Inexperience — He is new to the world. He hasn't yet faced life's trials or earned his place through hard work and time.
  • Maleness — The word is almost exclusively used for males. You would rarely, if ever, hear it applied to a girl or young woman.

All three qualities tend to come together. A stripling is young and lean and inexperienced — the whole package.

This is a word that carries a very specific emotional flavour, and understanding that flavour is key.

When someone calls a young male a stripling, they are almost always speaking from a position of being older, more experienced, or more powerful. The tone can go in two directions:

1. Dismissive or condescending — "He's just a stripling" means he's just a boy, barely worth taking seriously. He doesn't know what he doesn't know. An old general looking at a young recruit might use the word this way, with a slight shake of the head.

2. Affectionate or nostalgic — An older man remembering his own youth might say, "I was just a stripling back then," with warmth and a smile. Here, the word is gentle and fond, not insulting.

The word is never neutral. It always signals that the speaker sees the young person through the lens of age and experience.
How It Is Used in Sentences

Here are examples that show the word in action across different tones:

  • "When the war began, he was a mere stripling of sixteen, too young to shave." — Here it emphasises how heartbreakingly young he was.
  • "The old knight laughed when he saw his challenger. 'You send a stripling to fight me?'" — Dismissive and contemptuous.
  • "I remember my grandfather as a wise, strong man — it is strange to think he was once a stripling working in the fields." — Nostalgic and tender.
  • "The stripling stood nervously before the king, his voice still cracking between boy and man." — Vivid, literary, and slightly sympathetic.
Is It a Compliment or an Insult?

Neither, really — and both, depending on context. It is a descriptor, not an evaluation. But because it highlights youth and inexperience, it can be used as an insult (implying someone is too young and naive to be taken seriously) or as a compliment wrapped in nostalgia (implying someone was once fresh-faced and full of potential).

What it is not is a neutral, plain word like "teenager." It always carries a layer of perspective — usually the perspective of someone older looking at someone younger.
Where You Will Find This Word

Stripling is an old, literary word. You are most likely to encounter it in:

  • Classic and historical literature — novels set in medieval times, old war stories, Victorian fiction, biblical texts
  • Formal or elevated writing — speeches, essays, or prose that deliberately reaches for a more refined, old-fashioned register
  • Ironic or humorous modern use — someone today might call a 25-year-old colleague a stripling as a playful joke, especially if the speaker is much older

In everyday modern conversation, the word is rare. If someone uses it today without humour, they are almost certainly being deliberately literary or old-fashioned in their speech.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• Boy — Very plain and general. No implication of being on the edge of manhood.
  • Teenager — A neutral, modern, clinical label. No emotional colour at all.
  • Youth — Close in meaning, but more neutral and can be used in formal contexts without any nostalgic or condescending flavour.
  • Lad — Casual, friendly, and modern. No suggestion of slenderness or inexperience specifically.

Stripling is the only one of these that simultaneously paints a picture of physical leanness, youth, inexperience, and a perspective from above — all in a single word. That compression of meaning is what makes it unique and what has kept it alive in the language for so long.

If you had to compress the entire word into one sentence:

A stripling is a young, slim, inexperienced male who has crossed out of childhood but has not yet grown into full manhood — seen through the eyes of someone older and wiser.
15313:
To strive means to put in serious, sustained, and determined effort toward a goal — especially when it is difficult or takes a long time to achieve.

It is not just about trying something once. Strive suggests that you keep pushing, keep working hard, and don't give up easily. There is a sense of struggle and dedication built into the word.

She strives to be a better person every single day.

In that sentence, she is not just making a one-time effort. She is continuously working hard at it, day after day.

"Strive" carries a certain weight and seriousness. When you use it, you are saying that the effort is meaningful, persistent, and not easy. It suggests that the goal matters deeply to the person and that they are willing to face challenges to reach it.

Think of it this way: if "try" is turning a key in a lock once, "strive" is spending hours picking the lock, determined to open it no matter what.

Here is a simple scale to understand the intensity:

  • Try → a general, basic effort. Low pressure. "I'll try."
  • Strive → a serious, driven, ongoing effort against some difficulty. "I will keep working hard at this, no matter what."
  • Struggle → similar difficulty, but this word focuses more on how hard and painful the process is, rather than the goal.

So "strive" sits in the middle — it is more intense and serious than "try," but it focuses on your determined effort toward a goal rather than on your pain or suffering.

There are three main patterns:

1. Strive + to + verb (most common)
This is when you are working hard toward doing something.

He strives to improve his writing.
We must strive to treat everyone fairly.

2. Strive + for + noun
This is when you are working hard toward having or achieving something.

She strives for excellence in her work.
The team strives for perfection.

3. Strive + against + noun (less common)
This is when you are making a determined effort to fight or resist something.

They strived against injustice their whole lives.
He strives against his own bad habits.

SituationFormExample
General / habitstrive / strivesShe strives to be kind.
Right nowstrivingHe is striving to finish.
Paststrove or strivedThey strove / strived hard.
With "have/has/had"striven or strivedShe has striven all her life.

Quick note on past tense: Both strove and strived are correct for the simple past. Strove is more traditional and is more commonly used in formal or literary writing. Striven is the traditional past participle (used with "have"), but strived is also widely accepted.

He strove to succeed despite every obstacle. ✅
He strived to succeed despite every obstacle. ✅
She has striven her whole life for this moment. ✅

Here are examples across different situations so you can see the full range of the word:

Personal growth:

She strives to become a little better every day.

Work and achievement:

The company strives for customer satisfaction above everything else.

Difficult circumstances:

Even with very little money, he strove to give his children a good education.

Values and ideals:

A good leader strives to be honest, even when honesty is uncomfortable.

Ongoing effort:

Scientists are striving to find a cure for the disease.

Fighting against something:

She strived against self-doubt her entire career and eventually became one of the best in her field.
The Tone of the Word — When Do People Use It?

"Strive" is slightly formal. You would hear it in:

  • Speeches and motivational writing ("We must strive for a better world.")
  • Mission statements from companies or organizations ("We strive to deliver quality.")
  • Literature and serious writing
  • Inspirational and philosophical contexts

In casual, everyday conversation, people tend to say "try hard" or "work hard" instead. But "strive" is perfectly natural in slightly serious or thoughtful conversation too.
The One Thing That Makes "Strive" Unique

Many words describe effort — try, attempt, endeavor, aim. What makes strive special is the combination of three things happening at once:

  1. Serious effort — not a half-hearted try
  2. Persistence — it keeps going over time
  3. Difficulty — there is something to push against

If any one of those three things is missing, "strive" starts to feel like the wrong word. A casual, easy, one-time effort is not striving. Striving is what you do when something matters to you, it isn't easy, and you keep going anyway.
15314: The word stroke has many different meanings depending on the situation. But almost all of them share a common idea at their heart: a single, distinct action, movement, touch, or event. Once you feel that core idea, the many meanings become much easier to remember.
1. A Single Movement of the Body or a Tool

This is the most fundamental meaning. A stroke is one complete movement, especially one that is smooth and deliberate.

  • A swimmer makes strokes to move through the water — each pull of the arms is one stroke.
  • A painter makes brushstrokes — each sweep of the brush across a canvas is a stroke.
  • When you write or draw, the movement of your pen or pencil across the paper is a stroke.
  • In rowing, each pull of the oar through the water is a stroke.

Think of it this way: Anytime someone makes one clean, purposeful sweep — of an arm, a brush, a bat, or a pen — that's a stroke.
2. A Hit or Blow

A stroke can mean a single act of hitting something with force. This applies to both natural forces and physical actions.

  • A stroke of lightning = a single bolt of lightning that strikes.
  • A stroke of an axe = one swing of an axe hitting a tree.
  • A stroke of a whip = one crack of the whip.

In sports like tennis, golf, and cricket, a stroke is each individual hit of the ball. A golfer's score is often counted in strokes — how many times they hit the ball.
3. A Gentle Touch

Moving in the complete opposite direction from "a hard blow," a stroke can also mean a soft, slow, loving touch — the kind you give a pet or a child.

  • "She gave the cat a long, gentle stroke along its back."
  • "He felt the stroke of her hand on his cheek."

It describes the movement of your hand lightly gliding over a surface.
4. A Medical Emergency (A Brain Stroke)

In medicine, a stroke is a serious, sudden condition where blood flow to part of the brain is cut off, either because a blood vessel is blocked or because it bursts. Brain cells begin to die quickly without oxygen. This can cause sudden loss of speech, paralysis on one side of the body, confusion, or worse.

This meaning borrows from the older idea of being "struck down" suddenly — as if by an invisible blow. You may also hear it called a brain stroke or cerebrovascular accident (CVA).
5. A Stroke of Something — A Single Occurrence or Instance

The word is also used to describe a single, notable occurrence of something, especially something that happens suddenly or unexpectedly.

  • A stroke of luck = one sudden, unexpected piece of good fortune.
  • A stroke of genius = one brilliant, inspired idea that arrives suddenly.
  • A stroke of bad luck = one sudden unfortunate event.
  • A stroke of irony = a single, sharp moment of irony.

These phrases treat luck, genius, or misfortune the way you'd treat a bolt of lightning — something that strikes once, suddenly, and powerfully.
6. The Sound a Clock Makes

When a clock strikes (makes a sound to mark the hour), each individual chime is called a stroke.

  • "She arrived at the stroke of midnight." — meaning at the exact moment the clock chimed twelve.
  • "On the first stroke of ten, the ceremony began."

"At the stroke of" is a phrase meaning at the exact moment of a particular time.
7. A Line or Mark in Writing

In handwriting, typography, and calligraphy, a stroke is a single line that forms part of a letter or character.

  • The letter "T" has two strokes: a vertical one and a horizontal one across the top.
  • In Chinese or Japanese writing, characters are built from a specific number of strokes, and even the order in which you draw them matters.
  • A forward stroke (or just stroke in British English) refers to the punctuation mark / (the forward slash).
  • A backstroke in this context means \\.
8. In Engines — A Piston Stroke

Inside an engine, a stroke is one complete movement of a piston — either moving up or moving down inside a cylinder. This is why you hear of two-stroke and four-stroke engines — they describe how many piston movements it takes to complete one power cycle.
9. In Rowing — The Stroke (a Person)

In competitive rowing (crew), the rower who sits closest to the back of the boat (the stern) and faces the direction the boat is moving is called the stroke or stroke seat. This person sets the rhythm and pace that all other rowers must follow. Being the stroke is a position of great responsibility.
Pulling It All Together

Core IdeaExamples
One movement/sweepswimming stroke, brushstroke, pen stroke
One hit or blowstroke of lightning, axe stroke, golf stroke
A soft toucha stroke of the hand
A brain eventhaving a stroke
A single notable momentstroke of luck, stroke of genius
A clock chimeat the stroke of noon
A written linea stroke of a letter, a forward stroke (/)
A piston movementfour-stroke engine

The beauty of this word is that all its meanings radiate out from the same center: something singular, definite, and complete — whether it's one movement of your arm, one bolt of lightning, one brilliant idea, or one beat of a clock. Keep that image in mind, and every use of "stroke" will make sense immediately.
15315:
To stroke something means to move your hand gently and smoothly over a surface, usually in one repeated direction. Think of what you do when you pet a cat — you place your hand on its back and slide it forward, slowly and softly, again and again. That movement is a stroke. The key qualities of this action are: it is gentle, it is controlled, it is smooth (no rubbing back and forth quickly), and it is usually done with care or affection.

She stroked the dog's fur until it fell asleep.
He stroked his beard, thinking quietly.

The action doesn't have to be on a living thing. You can stroke a surface, a fabric, or an object — as long as the movement is that same slow, gentle glide.

She stroked the velvet gently, feeling its softness.
When It's Directed at a Person

When you stroke a person — their hair, face, arm, or hand — it almost always carries emotional warmth. It is a gesture of comfort, tenderness, or love. A mother strokes her child's forehead when the child is sick. A partner strokes the other's hand during a difficult moment. The action communicates: I am here, I care about you, you are safe. It is one of the most human gestures of reassurance.

She stroked his hair gently as he cried.
The nurse stroked the old man's hand and spoke softly to him.
The Figurative Meaning — Stroking Someone's Ego

Here is where the verb becomes more interesting. Because stroking someone physically makes them feel good and calm, the word is also used figuratively to describe saying or doing things that make someone feel important, admired, or special — even when your real intention is to please them, win their favour, or get something from them.

To stroke someone's ego means to flatter them, to tell them how great they are, to feed their pride. It often carries a slightly cunning or strategic flavour — you are not necessarily being totally sincere; you are managing the person's feelings deliberately.

The politician stroked the crowd with compliments before asking for their vote.
He knew how to stroke his boss's ego to get what he wanted.

Sometimes "stroke" is used on its own in this figurative sense, without the word "ego."

She stroked him with praise before delivering the bad news.

The logic here is beautiful once you see it: just as physical stroking soothes and pleases a person or animal, verbal stroking soothes and pleases a person's pride.

In several sports, "stroke" is used as a verb to mean to hit a ball with a smooth, controlled, deliberate motion — not a hard aggressive smash, but a clean, skilled strike where technique and timing matter.

In golf, you stroke the ball when you swing your club at it during normal play.
In cricket and tennis, a batsman or player strokes the ball when they hit it with clean, composed technique.
In swimming, to stroke means to perform the arm movements of a particular style — though this usage blurs into the noun form.

He stroked the ball perfectly into the far corner of the court.
She stroked a beautiful drive down the centre of the fairway.

The common thread in sports usage is always that same quality: smooth, controlled, deliberate — not wild or rushed.

In rowing, "to stroke a boat" or "to stroke a crew" means to row in the lead position — the rower at the end closest to the stern, whose rhythm every other rower in the boat must follow. To stroke here means to set the pace and style for everyone else.

He had stroked the Cambridge boat to victory three years in a row.

In some formal or older writing contexts, to stroke (or stroke out) a word or line means to draw a line through it to delete or cancel it. This is less common in everyday speech, but you may encounter it in legal or editing contexts.

Please stroke out the incorrect entry and write the correct one above it.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

One of the most important things to understand about this verb is its tone. "Stroke" almost always implies something soft, deliberate, and careful. It is never a rough, hurried, or careless action. Whether someone is stroking a cat, stroking a person's hair, stroking a golf ball, or stroking someone's ego, there is always a sense of intention, lightness, and smoothness behind it. This is what separates it from similar words like "rub," "scratch," "pat," or "brush."

  • Rub = back and forth, often with friction or pressure.
  • Pat = a short, gentle tap, not a sliding motion.
  • Brush = a quick, light sweeping movement, often to remove something.
  • Stroke = a slow, deliberate, tender glide in one direction.

To stroke is to move your hand (or something else) slowly, gently, and smoothly over a surface — and by extension, to treat someone's feelings with the same gentle, deliberate care, usually to soothe, comfort, or win them over.

Once you hold that image in your mind — the slow, soft, careful glide — every use of this verb, whether physical or figurative, in sports or in conversation, will make immediate sense.
15316:
To stroll means to walk slowly and in a relaxed, easy way — usually because you are enjoying yourself or simply have no reason to hurry.

It is not just any kind of walking. Every time you use the word stroll, it carries three invisible messages at once:

  • The pace is slow.
  • The mood is calm and comfortable.
  • There is no urgency — you are not trying to reach somewhere fast.

Think of someone walking through a park on a sunny afternoon, hands in pockets, looking around at the trees and flowers. That is a perfect stroll. Now imagine someone rushing through the same park because they are late for a meeting. That is not a stroll at all — even though both people are walking.
What Makes It Different from Just "Walking"

The word walk is neutral. It simply tells you that someone is moving on foot. It says nothing about speed or mood.

Stroll is a specific type of walking. It always adds meaning. The moment you say someone is strolling, the listener automatically pictures a calm, unhurried, pleasant scene.

Here is a simple contrast:

  • "She walked to the store." → We only know she went there on foot. Maybe she was rushing. Maybe she was calm. We don't know.
  • "She strolled to the store." → We now know she was in no hurry. She was relaxed. The walk itself was pleasant.
How It Feels From the Inside

When you stroll, you are not focused on arriving somewhere. You are, in a sense, enjoying the act of walking itself. You might be looking around, thinking quietly, chatting with a friend, or simply breathing in the fresh air. Your body is loose and comfortable, not tense. Your mind is at ease.

This is why people often stroll after a meal, on a holiday, by the sea, or in a garden. These are moments when life slows down and you have nothing pressing to do.

These sentences show how the word is used naturally:

  • "We strolled along the riverbank for an hour before heading home."
  • "He strolled through the market, stopping now and then to look at things."
  • "On Sunday mornings, they love to stroll around the old part of the city."
  • "The children strolled home from school, kicking leaves along the way."
  • "She strolled into the café and ordered a coffee without a care in the world."

Notice how in every sentence, there is a feeling of ease and gentleness. No one is rushing. No one is stressed.

Sometimes, stroll is used figuratively — meaning it is not describing actual walking, but something done very easily and without effort, almost as if you are casually walking through it.

  • "He strolled through the interview." → He found the interview so easy that it felt effortless, like a relaxed walk.
  • "She strolled into the finals without dropping a single game." → She moved through the competition with ease and confidence.
  • "The champion strolled to victory." → She won without being truly challenged.

This usage often carries a slight tone of admiration — it suggests someone is so skilled or confident that a challenging situation feels like nothing to them.

There is also a related, slightly negative use:

  • "He strolled in forty minutes late." → Here, strolled emphasizes that the person walked in calmly and casually, showing no awareness of — or concern about — being very late. It implies a kind of careless arrogance.
Words That Are Similar (and How They Differ)

Understanding stroll more deeply means knowing how it sits among its neighbors.

Wander means to walk with no clear direction or destination. A person who wanders might not even know where they are going. Strolling is more intentional — you are relaxed, but you generally know where you are or where you are headed.

Saunter is very close to stroll. Both suggest a slow, relaxed walk. However, saunter often carries a slightly stronger suggestion of confidence, self-assurance, or even a touch of showing off. You saunter when you feel cool and unhurried in a way that others might notice.

Amble is also similar — a gentle, easy walk. It is slightly more old-fashioned in everyday speech than stroll.

March is the opposite energy entirely — it is fast, deliberate, and purposeful, often with a military feel.

Rush or hurry is the full opposite of stroll — all urgency, no relaxation.

Among all of these, stroll is by far the most common and natural word to use in everyday English for a slow, pleasant, relaxed walk.
Where and When People Use It

Stroll fits beautifully in peaceful, pleasant, or leisurely settings:

  • Along a beach, river, or lake.
  • Through a park, garden, or forest path.
  • Around a town square, market, or old neighborhood.
  • On a quiet evening after dinner.
  • On a lazy holiday afternoon.

It would sound strange to say someone strolled through a dangerous situation, a stressful scene, or while clearly panicking — unless it is being used figuratively (as in the competition example above) to show that someone is so capable that they feel no stress at all.
The Overall Feeling of the Word

If you had to capture stroll in a feeling, it would be: unhurried freedom. It is the walk of someone who has time, who is at peace, and who is — at least for that moment — simply enjoying being alive and moving through the world at their own pace.

"Strong" describes something — a person, object, smell, argument, feeling, or situation — that has a high degree of power, force, or intensity, and that holds up well or makes a significant impact as a result.

Two ideas are almost always present:

  • It has a lot of something (power, force, intensity, concentration)
  • It doesn't give way easily, or it has a powerful effect on other things

One or both of these ideas run through every use of the word.

1. Physical Power

The most familiar use. A person, animal, or body part that can exert great force.

She is incredibly strong — she can carry a bag that most people can barely lift.
He has strong arms from years of working on a farm.
The horse is strong enough to pull a heavy cart.

It also describes a body that is healthy and not fragile:

After weeks of rest, she's growing stronger every day.

2. Structural Strength (Objects and Materials)

An object or material is "strong" if it resists breaking, bending, or damage under pressure.

Use strong rope — a thin one will snap under the weight.
The bridge is strong enough to carry heavy trucks.
She wore strong boots that wouldn't tear easily.

The idea here is durability — the thing doesn't give way under stress.

3. Mental and Emotional Strength

A person is emotionally or mentally "strong" if they can face difficulty, pain, or pressure without falling apart.

She stayed strong even after losing everything she had worked for.
You need to be mentally strong to compete at that level.
It takes a strong character to admit when you are wrong.

This sense is about resilience — the ability to endure without collapsing.

4. Powerful in Effect or Influence

Something "strong" here has a large impact, makes a real difference, or is hard to dismiss or ignore.

Arguments and evidence:

That's a strong argument — it's difficult to find a flaw in it.
The evidence against him is very strong.

Leaders and personalities:

She is a strong leader who makes decisions clearly and confidently.
He has a strong personality — people notice him in any room.

Economics and organizations:

The country has a strong economy.
They have a strong team this season.

The idea: it carries real weight, it matters, it cannot easily be set aside.

5. High Intensity or Concentration

"Strong" describes things that are intense, potent, or concentrated — not faint, mild, or diluted.

  • Strong coffee — has a lot of caffeine; the taste is rich and powerful, not watered down.
  • A strong smell — it hits you powerfully; you cannot miss it.
  • A strong wind — blowing with significant, noticeable force.
  • Strong light — very bright, possibly uncomfortable to look at directly.
  • A strong color — vivid and deep, not pale or washed out.
  • Strong medicine — potent; it has a powerful effect on the body.
  • Strong alcohol — high in alcohol content.

The strong smell of onions filled the entire kitchen.
Don't drink that — it's very strong.

6. Firm Beliefs, Feelings, and Opinions

When someone holds a belief or feeling very deeply and firmly, we call it strong.

She has strong opinions about how children should be raised.
He felt a strong sense of loyalty to his old friends.
There is strong opposition to the new law.
I have a strong feeling that something is wrong here.

Here, "strong" means: not weak, not uncertain, not easily shaken or changed. The feeling or view is felt deeply and held firmly.

7. Numbers and Size of Groups

"Strong" is placed after a number to describe the size of a group.

A crowd a thousand strong gathered in the square.
(= A crowd of one thousand people)

It also signals "above expectations" or "performing impressively" in numbers:

Strong sales figures. A strong majority. Strong test scores.

8. Healthy and Doing Well

In everyday speech, "strong" describes someone who is healthy enough to function, or something that is performing well.

She's strong enough to go back to work now.
The business has been going strong for over a decade.
Their performance this quarter has been strong.

Strong language — rude, offensive, or profane words.

The film contains strong language and is not suitable for children.

Strong point / strong suit — something you are especially good at.

Patience is not my strong point.

Strong stomach — the ability to handle disturbing or disgusting things without feeling sick or upset.

You need a strong stomach to watch that documentary.

Strong-willed — determined; not easily talked out of your decisions.

She's strong-willed — once she decides something, that's it.

Going strong — continuing to succeed or function well, often over a long time.

They've been married for forty years and are still going strong.

Come on strong — to behave very intensely or aggressively toward someone, especially when first meeting them.

He came on too strong and made her feel uncomfortable.

Strong-arm (someone) — to force someone to do something using threats or pressure.

They strong-armed him into signing the contract.

The strong silent type — a person (often used for men) who is tough and dependable but quiet and reserved by nature.

As strong as an ox — a common comparison meaning extremely physically strong.

"Strong" adjusts in degree naturally:

stronger than expected / the strongest argument / not strong enough / as strong as an ox

You can also use adverbs with it:

very strong, incredibly strong, reasonably strong, fairly strong, surprisingly strong

• It does not always mean physically powerful. A strong smell, a strong argument, or a strong feeling have nothing to do with muscle.
  • It does not mean aggressive or harsh — though it can describe things with intense effects.
  • It does not mean "big" or "large." A small person can be very strong. A short sentence can be the strongest argument in a debate.
The Thread That Ties It All Together

No matter which use you encounter, "strong" always signals that something is above average in power, intensity, or resistance — and because of that, it has a real, noticeable effect on the world around it. Something strong does not fade quietly into the background. It holds, it impacts, it matters.
15318:
A stronghold is a place that is so well-protected, so deeply rooted, or so dominant that it is extremely hard to attack, remove, or change.

Think of it this way: imagine a heavily walled castle sitting on top of a hill, surrounded by a moat. Enemies struggle to get in. The people inside feel safe and powerful. That castle is a stronghold. The word carries that same spirit — of strength, dominance, and resistance — in everything it describes.

The word works on two levels, and you'll encounter both constantly.

1. The Literal Meaning — A Fortified Physical Place

In its most direct sense, a stronghold is a physical place built or used to be defended and protected — somewhere that is very hard for an enemy to capture. It is a safe and powerful base.

  • A castle, a fortress, a bunker, a walled city — these are classic strongholds.
  • In modern times, it can refer to a military base, a rebel hideout deep in the mountains, or any heavily guarded territory.

Examples:

  • "The army attacked the enemy's stronghold in the hills."
  • "The rebels used the old fort as their stronghold for years."
  • "The general retreated to his last stronghold as the city fell."

The key feeling here is: it is hard to break into, and the people there feel powerful and protected.

2. The Figurative Meaning — A Place Where Something is Dominant and Deeply Rooted

This is where the word becomes truly rich and useful. A stronghold doesn't always have walls or soldiers. In everyday modern language, it is used to describe a place, group, or area where a particular idea, belief, political view, culture, religion, or group is dominant, deeply established, and very hard to challenge or change.

Here, the "fortress" is not made of stone — it is made of loyalty, tradition, deep belief, or numbers.

Examples:

  • "That rural state has been a stronghold of conservative politics for decades." — Meaning: conservative politics is so dominant and deeply rooted there that it is very hard to shift.
  • "The university is a stronghold of scientific research." — Meaning: science thrives there; it is a powerful center of it.
  • "The mountains remained a stronghold of the old religion long after the rest of the country had converted."
  • "The gang controlled that neighborhood — it was their stronghold."

The key feeling here is: something has such a firm grip on a place or group that it won't easily be shaken or replaced.
The One Feeling That Ties Both Meanings Together

Whether you're talking about a castle or a political region, a stronghold always gives you the same feeling:

"This thing — whether it's a place, a group, an idea, or a belief — is powerful here, deeply entrenched, and not going down without a serious fight."

It implies strength, dominance, and resistance to outside pressure.
Shades and Nuances You Should Know

It can be used positively or negatively, depending on your perspective.

  • To the people inside, a stronghold is a place of safety, power, and pride.
  • To the people trying to challenge it, a stronghold is an obstacle — a stubborn, hard-to-crack center of opposition.

The word itself is neutral. Whether it sounds good or bad depends entirely on which side of the wall you're on.

"Last stronghold" is a very common and powerful phrase.
When almost everything has been lost, defeated, or changed, and only one place remains — that final place is called the last stronghold. It carries a dramatic, often desperate feeling.

  • "The library was the last stronghold of quiet in the noisy city."
  • "The village was the last stronghold of the ancient language."

The thing being "held" in a stronghold doesn't have to be good.
A criminal gang can have a stronghold. A corrupt regime can have a stronghold. The word describes dominance and deep-rootedness — not moral goodness.

If you ever forget the meaning, just split the word:

STRONG + HOLD

Something has a strong hold on a place — physically, politically, culturally, or ideologically. It grips it tightly and won't let go easily. That's your stronghold.

Before anything else, hold onto this single sentence, because it is the heart of the word:

A structure is something — or the internal arrangement of something — where multiple parts are organized in a deliberate, meaningful way to form a coherent whole.

Every use of "structure," in every field and every context, is a variation of this idea. The arrangement is never random. It is always purposeful. And that arrangement is precisely what makes the thing what it is. Once you truly understand this, every new encounter with the word will make immediate sense.

"Structure" as a noun works in two major ways.

The first is a physical, constructed thing. Here, "structure" refers to a tangible object you can see and touch — something that was built by assembling parts together in a specific way. Buildings, bridges, tunnels, towers, and dams are all structures. A beehive is a structure. A spider's web is a structure. What qualifies something as a "structure" in this sense is that it was constructed, and its parts hold a defined relationship to one another. You might say, "The engineers inspected the crumbling structure," or "The ancient structure had stood for two thousand years." In everyday speech, "structure" in this sense is more formal and technical than simply saying "building."

The second is the invisible internal arrangement of something. This is the more widely used, more powerful sense of the word, and it has nothing to do with a physical object. Here, "structure" refers to the framework — the pattern, the organization, the way parts relate to each other — that exists inside something non-physical. When a teacher says your essay lacks structure, they don't mean the paper itself is falling apart. They mean that your ideas are not arranged in a logical, coherent order. When a scientist talks about the structure of a DNA molecule, they mean the specific way its chemical components are arranged and bonded together. When a manager talks about a company's structure, they mean how roles, departments, and reporting relationships are organized.

In all of these cases, "structure" is answering one fundamental question: how are the parts arranged in relation to each other, and what does that arrangement achieve?

Structure is not merely decorative. It is functional. It is what holds something together and makes it work.

A house without a proper structure collapses under its own weight. An essay without structure is a jumble of ideas that the reader cannot follow. A company without structure is a group of people with no clarity about who does what. A DNA molecule without its precise structure cannot carry genetic information. In every case, it is the structure — the arrangement of parts — that gives the whole thing its form, its strength, and its purpose.

This leads to one of the most important truths about the word: if you change the structure of something, you change the thing itself. Rearrange the atoms in a molecule and you get a completely different substance. Rearrange the chapters of a novel and you tell a completely different story. The content may be the same, but the structure is different, and so the thing becomes different.
How the Word Appears Across Different Areas of Life

Because the concept is so universal — parts organized into a whole — "structure" turns up in virtually every area of human knowledge and activity.

In language and writing, the structure of a sentence refers to the grammatical arrangement of its words: which part is the subject, which is the verb, which is the object, and how clauses connect. The structure of a piece of writing — an essay, a report, a novel — refers to how its sections, paragraphs, and ideas are logically ordered and sequenced.

In business and organizations, every company or institution has a structure that defines how it operates: who reports to whom, how decisions are made, and how work is divided. You will often hear the phrase "organizational structure" or "corporate structure."

In science, biologists study the structure of living things — the arrangement of organs inside a body, or the arrangement of components inside a cell. Chemists study molecular structure, meaning the precise way atoms are bonded and arranged in a substance.

In music, a song or symphony has a structure — the way its sections (verses, choruses, movements) are ordered and how they relate to create the whole piece.

In society, sociologists speak of social structure, referring to the organized patterns of relationships between people, institutions, and social groups — the invisible framework that shapes how a society operates.

In everyday personal life, someone might say that their daily routine gives them structure, meaning a reliable, organized framework for their day that keeps them productive and grounded.

One important and subtle use of the word is when it appears without any article — without "a" or "the" — and without a plural form. In this case, "structure" refers to the abstract quality of being organized. It refers to the presence (or absence) of deliberate arrangement in general.

For example: "This essay lacks structure" does not mean the essay is missing a specific structure. It means the essay is disorganized — it has no clear internal arrangement at all. Similarly, "Children thrive with structure" means children do well when their days have a reliable, organized routine. And "We need to bring some structure to this project" means the project needs to be organized more deliberately.

In this uncountable use, "structure" is the concept of order itself — the idea of things being intentionally arranged rather than chaotic.

To sharpen your understanding, a few clear distinctions are worth knowing.

Structure is not the same as content. The content of something is what it contains — the ideas, the materials, the information. The structure is how those things are arranged. An essay about climate change and an essay about cooking could have exactly the same structure (introduction, three main points, conclusion) while having completely different content. Conversely, two essays could contain the same ideas but present them in completely different orders, giving them different structures.

Structure is not the same as appearance or style. A bridge can be elegant or ugly, large or small. Those are qualities of appearance. The structure refers to how its steel beams, cables, and supports are arranged to hold the weight. Appearance and structure can influence each other, but they are different things.

And finally, a random pile of things is not a structure. A pile of bricks is not a structure. The moment those bricks are deliberately arranged into a wall — with each brick placed in a specific relationship to the others — you have a structure. The deliberateness, the intentionality of the arrangement, is essential to the word.
The Word in a Single Sentence

If you need to carry one sentence in your mind forever:

A structure is a physical construction, or the internal arrangement of any system, in which parts are organized in a specific, purposeful way — and it is precisely that organization that gives the whole thing its form, its stability, and its function.

Whenever you meet the word, ask yourself: what are the parts, and how are they arranged? That question will always unlock the meaning.
